newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-CANTONA'S TURBULENT CAREER COMES TO ABRUPT END.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CANTONA'S TURBULENT CAREER COMES TO ABRUPT END.

text.p: Eric Cantona's retirement from professional soccer brings a brilliant, turbulent career to an abrupt end.
After a mediocre season, there had been plenty of speculation the Frenchman would leave Old Trafford after five monumental seasons with Manchester United.
Some said he would return to French football, others said the 30-year-old, still at the peak of his idiosyncratic game, would head for Japan.
Instead, United revealed on Sunday that Cantona was apparently turning his back on the game he has always played with a passion -- sometimes played with a fury.
Millions of fans around the world know Cantona as a gifted, brilliant artist capable of the most sublime skills.
But most of those millions also recognise the flaws that may always keep him out of the pantheon of the greats -- the petulance, the niggling fouls, the sly kicks at an opponent.
He played the best football of his colourful 13-year career in England.
But even here, he will be remembered above all for the astonishing and ugly "kung-fu" kick on a fan in 1995 -- an aberration which earned him a eight-month ban from soccer.
When he re-emerged early in the 1995-96 season he appeared to be a different man -- the temper had been tamed.
Nevertheless, the talent was still pure Cantona and he became England's Footballer of the Year in his first season back from the wilderness as United claimed their third title in four years.
This season Cantona appeared at times to have lost his touch. Even so, his cult status among the United faithful remained intact.
The Frenchman has been in trouble with soccer's authorities many times.

There are famous stories of him screaming the word "Idiot" in the face of every member of a French disciplinary committee who were about to ban him for a month. They ended up by doubling his suspension. Cantona responded by announcing his retirement, only to surface a year later in England on a trial with Sheffield Wednesday.
In France, Cantona had punch-ups with team mates, threw his shirt at the national team boss, argued with referees, argued with his bosses, insulted journalists and was sent off.
He once summed up his maverick philosophy of life with the phrase: "Regrets? I regret nothing -- good or bad."
Alex Ferguson, his manager at United, said of him: "He's complicated. Perhaps he is too quiet and emotional -- maybe he bottles things up.
"He can go out and do something crazy, something nobody in his right mind would condone.
"Then he resolves to exact his own justice, which is madness. It is also usually so blatant it is instantly self-destructive.
"His worst offences are certainly not premeditated or in any way calculated."
In his book "My Story", Cantona spoke of his heroes -- rock star Jim Morrison of The Doors, the poet Arthur Rimbaud, anarchist singer Leo Ferre.
Pat Crerand, who won the European Cup with United in 1968, said: "People in Manchester will be in a state of total mourning.
"I can't believe it, but Eric's that type of person. He's very brave and courageous. He's done it with a great deal of dignity but it's a shock to everyone in Manchester.
"People will be disappointed that they can't go to Old Trafford and see him running out on to the pitch for a last time.
"He'll go down along with the Busby Babes, Sir Matt Busby, Denis Law, Sir Bobby Charlton -- he's there alongside all of them.
And Crerand said Cantona was not the type of man to reverse his decision to retire.
"He's a very mature and a very intelligent man and obviously he's got something up his sleeve, though I don't know what it is," he said.
"I don't think we'll see him back as a player."
